bibliographic.title: Consumers and Artificial Intelligence: An Experiential Perspective
bibliographic.authors: Stefano Puntoni; Rebecca Walker Reczek; Markus Giesler; Simona Botti
bibliographic.citation_apa: Puntoni, S., Walker Reczek, R., Giesler, M., & Botti, S. (2018). Consumers and artificial intelligence: An experiential perspective. [Venue unclear].

methodology.method_family: conceptual framework integrating sociological and psychological scholarship
methodology.study_design: theoretical framework paper identifying four consumer experience types with illustrative examples
methodology.sample_description: no empirical sample; uses illustrative consumer anecdotes and secondary examples
methodology.technology_context: consumer-facing AI including wearables, recommender systems, smart household products, voice-activated virtual assistants, chatbots, and social AI interactions

eligibility.decision_rationale: The paper offers a pre-LLM conceptual framework for consumer interactions with AI, including chatbots and voice assistants, and discusses policy, privacy, discrimination, and trust. It does not address LLM-based conversational systems or operational governance mechanisms in regulated high-stakes deployments, so it is better treated as foundational contextual evidence than central evidence for the review.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Python metadata mis-extracted the title; venue and peer-review status are unclear from the excerpt, and keyword overlap may overstate fit to LLM conversational governance in regulated settings.

appraisal.notes: Strong conceptual clarity and fit for a framework paper, but limited empirical sampling, transparent data collection, and direct operational governance evidence.

cerqual.explanation: The framework is internally coherent and adequately developed for consumer AI experiences, but methodological limitations are notable because claims rely on illustrative examples rather than systematic evidence, and relevance to LLM conversational governance in regulated environments is only partial.

axial_codes: bias and accountability in automated interactions
coding.theme: Experiential costs and benefits of consumer-facing AI
coding.subtheme: Social experiences with chatbots and voice assistants

synthesis.main_claim: Consumer interactions with AI create experiential value and costs across four types of experiences—data-capture, classification, delegation, and social—and organizations should address social and individual challenges rather than treating AI only as a neutral efficiency tool.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a parsimonious experiential framework for understanding chatbots, voice assistants, and other consumer AI interactions, linking them to policy and managerial responses around privacy, discrimination, replacement, and alienation.
synthesis.limitations: Conceptual agenda-setting paper without systematic empirical testing; additional consumer experiences remain uncharted; technology context predates LLMs and does not specify operational governance controls.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual background on social conversational AI experiences, consumer trust/accountability concerns, and high-level policy implications; not as primary evidence on LLM conversational governance, guardrails, observability, audit, or compliance in regulated deployments.

evidence.claim: Paper is tied to a 2018 MSI Scholars conference opportunity
evidence.excerpt: The authors thank Carl Mela and the Marketing Science Institute for organizing the 2018 MSI Scholars conference that provided the opportunity to work together on this project

evidence.claim: Research is conceptual and aims to bridge technical and social perspectives
evidence.excerpt: this approach does not consider the social and individual challenges that can occur when AI is deployed. This research aims to bridge these two perspectives

evidence.claim: Framework identifies four consumer experience types
evidence.excerpt: we identify four types of consumer experiences with AI: (1) data-capture, (2) classification, (3) delegation, and (4) social.
This approach allows us to discuss policy and managerial avenues to address the ways in which consumers may fail to experience value

evidence.claim: Includes voice-activated virtual assistants as a consumer AI context

evidence.excerpt: Keywords: artificial intelligence, AI, customer experience, technology marketing, Internet of Things, privacy, discrimination, replacement, alienation

evidence.claim: Examples span health monitoring and voice assistants
evidence.excerpt: health monitoring with wearable devices, advice with recommender systems, peace of mind with smart household products, and convenience with voice-activated virtual assistants.

evidence.claim: Social experience includes known AI voice assistants and organizational chatbots
evidence.excerpt: when consumers know at the outset that the interaction partner is an AI, such as when using a voice assistant like Apple’s Siri, and when they interact with an AI representing an organization without necessarily knowing initially that it is non-human, such as when receiving customer service from an automated chatbot.

evidence.claim: Anthropomorphic cues affect trust and perceived risk in virtual assistant interactions
evidence.excerpt: anthropomorphic cues increase trust towards self-driving cars (Waytz, Heafner, and Epley 2014) and reduce perceived risk when consumers are in a position of power (Kim and McGill 2011), as when they interact with a virtual assistant.

evidence.claim: Failed chatbot service can alienate consumers
evidence.excerpt: The first type can occur with any failed automated customer service, as exemplified in this exchange between a customer and chatbot UX Bear

evidence.claim: Chatbots can reproduce societal discrimination, exemplified by Tay
evidence.excerpt: chatbots programmed without considering how existing discrimination in society may affect their operation, such as when Tay, a Twitter bot by Microsoft, began offering white supremacist answers to users soon after its launch

evidence.claim: Personal virtual assistants can reflect sexist cultural narratives
evidence.excerpt: The cultural narratives of oppression and discrimination underlying this example are even more apparent in the context of personal virtual assistants.

evidence.claim: Framework applies to personal virtual assistants among other contexts
evidence.excerpt: Our framework offers a parsimonious template to conceptualize how consumers navigate the disparate consumption contexts powered by AI, including social media, online shopping, and personal virtual assistants.

evidence.claim: Conclusion positions chatbots among consumer-facing AI heralded as social good
evidence.excerpt: Consumer-facing AI products and services such as college application software, chatbots, and knowledge aggregators have been heralded as forces for good
